analysis.title: GS MarketStrats: The Price of Capital
key_insights: Follow-up to 'The Price of Credibility'. Fiscal expansion in the US, Europe and Japan plus the AI investment boom created scarcity of capital and pushed real rates higher. The question now is who gets rationed first as the cost of capital rises.

Base case: higher real rates are beginning to slow private demand and challenge the most capital-intensive parts of the AI ecosystem. This does not automatically produce an unconstrained bull market in duration, because sovereign borrowing, defence commitments and refinancing needs are hard to postpone.

Recent price action: long-end yields have rallied despite firm inflation data, while AI-linked equities and parts of hyperscaler credit have weakened. Markets are testing whether economies and companies can absorb the current cost of capital, not declaring victory over inflation.

Reflexive loop: AI optimism drives investment and demand for capital, which supports nominal growth, which with capital scarcity pushes real rates higher. Higher hurdle rates then challenge AI valuations, credit and capex.

Markets are testing whether AI accounted for a disproportionate share of the improvement in US growth expectations. Reassessing AI would mean reassessing part of the US exceptionalism narrative and the real-rate equilibrium built around it.

An AI buildout delivered over ten years rather than three could produce a similar stock of infrastructure but would mean less near-term capital demand, less support for nominal growth and less upward pressure on equilibrium real rates.

The demand for capital may slow but the need for capital may not. US deficits, European defence and infrastructure, and Japanese sovereign financing needs could leave a floor beneath global yields, so a weaker AI cycle does not return markets to the 2010s low-rate world.
The adjustment is more likely to fall on households and the most capital-intensive, longest-duration private investments than on governments.

Yields rallied despite a stronger inflation print because markets are focusing on transmission: current real rates may already be restrictive enough to slow investment, challenge AI capex and weaken nominal growth. The duration rally is not guaranteed to be durable.

Regional view: US duration has the clearest route to rally if AI investment and US exceptionalism are downgraded. European duration benefits from weaker growth but is constrained by defence, infrastructure and energy-security spending. Japanese duration stays exposed to policy normalisation and heavy financing needs.

Oil is the constraint variable. If oil falls, capital demand and inflation fall and central banks can validate lower real rates. If oil stays elevated, growth can weaken before inflation normalises, creating a stagflationary tail.

Dollar: lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar can persist while markets price an orderly US growth moderation. If weaker growth broadens into credit stress, the likelier configuration is lower yields, wider spreads, weaker equities and a stronger dollar.

Three scenarios: (1) capital remains scarce, AI weakness is only a valuation adjustment, duration rally fades and the dollar stays supported. (2) Higher real rates work (base case): US duration performs, the dollar weakens, persistent fiscal demand limits the fall in global yields. (3) AI was the marginal growth story: yields fall, AI leadership breaks, credit spreads widen, and the dollar weakens first then strengthens if risk-off.

sector_views.rationale: Higher real rates raise hurdle rates for the most capital-intensive, longest-duration AI investments. AI equities and hyperscaler credit have already weakened, and the report says AI may be one of the first casualties of the rates already in place.

macro_indicators.reading: Elevated, described as potentially restrictive enough to slow investment (no level cited)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Higher real rates are beginning to slow private demand and challenge AI capex. In the base case they work to slow housing, credit creation and corporate investment.

macro_indicators.reading: Described as exceptionally strong (no figure cited)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Strong nominal growth helped justify higher yields, and the report asks how much of it was driven by AI. In the base case it converges toward trend.

macro_indicators.reading: Firm / stronger inflation print (no figure cited)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Long-end yields rallied despite the firm print, which suggests markets are pricing growth and transmission risks over inflation.
Oil is the constraint variable. If it stays elevated, growth can weaken before inflation normalises, creating a stagflationary tail.

trade_ideas.description: Long US duration (base case: US duration performs as higher real rates slow private demand)
trade_ideas.rationale: Higher real rates slow housing, credit creation and corporate investment, and the US has the clearest route to a duration rally if AI investment and US exceptionalism are downgraded.
trade_ideas.risk: If US growth merely moderates and AI investment reaccelerates, markets could rediscover the capital-scarcity argument. Fiscal deficits and sovereign issuance could also limit the decline in yields.

trade_ideas.description: Weaker US dollar in the base case (lower Treasury yields, orderly moderation in US growth)
trade_ideas.rationale: The combination of lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar can persist while markets price an orderly moderation in US growth.
trade_ideas.risk: If weaker growth broadens into credit stress, the dollar strengthens on safe-haven demand.

risk_factors: AI investment reaccelerates while US growth only moderates, reviving the capital-scarcity argument and pushing yields back up
Sticky oil prices create a stagflationary tail in which growth slows before inflation gives central banks room to respond
Growth weakness broadens into credit stress, widening spreads and weakening equities
Persistent sovereign borrowing and issuance in the US, Europe and Japan keep a floor under global yields
Hyperscaler capex proves less immediate or less profitable than expected
geopolitical: Europe is increasing defence, energy security and infrastructure spending and faces market-imposed limits to fiscal expansion
Japan faces substantial sovereign financing needs as its interest-rate regime normalises

tension_points.bull_case: AI investment continues broadly as planned, US nominal growth stays resilient and governments keep absorbing savings. Recent AI weakness is a valuation adjustment, real rates stay elevated and the dollar stays supported.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher real rates raise hurdle rates and the AI buildout proves less immediate or less profitable than expected. Nominal growth weakens, Treasury yields fall, AI equity leadership breaks and credit spreads widen.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If US growth merely moderates and AI investment reaccelerates, markets could quickly rediscover the original capital-scarcity argument and the duration rally would fade.

tension_points.bull_case: Real rates are already restrictive enough to slow investment and nominal growth, so US duration can rally and the dollar weaken.
tension_points.bear_case: Fiscal deficits, sovereign issuance and global financing needs have not disappeared and leave a floor beneath global yields.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reacceleration in AI investment alongside only moderate US growth, or oil staying elevated so that inflation limits central bank easing.

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher real rates are beginning to slow private demand and challenge the most capital-intensive parts of the AI ecosystem.
Governments are unlikely to stop borrowing, so persistent sovereign demand for capital limits how far global yields can fall.
theme_stances.evidence: The demand for capital may slow. The need for capital may not.
